approachQuestion.prompt:
Middle calibration value

Two instruments provide read-only random-access arrays A and B, each sorted in nondecreasing order. Their combined number of readings is odd. Return the single middle value in their combined sorted multiset, counting duplicates as separate readings.

Constraints: 0 <= m=A.length <= n=B.length <= 200000; m+n >= 1 is odd; values are signed 32-bit integers. Prefer the smallest worst-case number of probes as a function of both lengths, then least working memory.

Examples: A=[2,9], B=[1,3,7] -> 3; A=[], B=[4,4,8] -> 4; A=[1,1], B=[1,5,6] -> 1.
constraints: Inputs may contain duplicates and A may be empty.
Return a scalar value; do not modify either input.

options.text: Let L=(m+n+1)/2. Binary-search the count i taken from A into a left partition, with j=L-i from B. Use conceptual negative/positive infinity at empty boundaries. Accept when A-left<=B-right and B-left<=A-right; return max(A-left,B-left). If A-left>B-right decrease i, otherwise increase it.
options.feedback: A is the shorter array, so all searched i from 0 through m give legal j. The cross-boundary inequalities establish that all L left values precede the right values; their maximum is the odd-length median. Failed inequalities determine which direction can restore the ordering.

options.text: Apply the same partition search recursively over integer bounds for i, without copying either input.
options.feedback: The cross-boundary test and directions are valid, but recursive frames are avoidable working memory. The iterative implementation has the same probe bound with fixed storage.

options.text: Advance two sorted-array pointers, consuming the smaller current reading until the combined middle position is reached.
options.feedback: This gives the right median and can use fixed storage, but it may consume half of all readings even when A is tiny. Partition search needs far fewer worst-case probes for such inputs.

options.text: Take the middle value of each nonempty input and return the smaller of those two values; for an empty A return B's middle.
options.feedback: For A=[2,9], B=[1,3,7], taking floor(length/2) within each array gives 9 and 3 and happens to work. But A=[1,2], B=[8,9,10] yields min(2,9)=2 instead of the correct 8. Individual middles do not determine the combined rank.

feedback.reason: Put exactly L=(m+n+1)/2 readings on the left by choosing i from A and L-i from B. Search i in the shorter array. A partition is valid when neither left boundary exceeds the opposite right boundary. Move i left if A contributes too-large a left boundary, otherwise right. At a valid partition return the larger left boundary; treat absent boundaries as conceptual infinities without overflowing integer sentinels.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Analyze only partition-search implemented iteratively on A, the shorter array. Let m=A.length and n=B.length, with m<=n. Empty boundaries use constant-time checks, not actual out-of-range reads. Comparisons, length arithmetic, and random access are constant time. No merging, copying, hashing, or recursion is used. Include the constant work when m=0. Choose the tightest pair.
constraints: Use worst-case bounds. Count all working memory including any stack; exclude supplied inputs and the scalar result.

options.text: O(m + n) time, O(1) auxiliary space

feedback.reason: Search m+1 cuts of the shorter input with fixed boundary comparisons.
details: There are m+1 possible cuts in the shorter array. Constant-many cross-boundary reads validate each cut, and each failed test halves the cut interval. This gives O(1+log(m+1)) time and O(1) auxiliary space, including an empty shorter array.
“O(log(m + 1) + 1) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: The search has m+1 possible cut counts and constant boundary work; empty A takes constant time.
“O(m + n) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: A linear merge would inspect both arrays, but cut search probes only the shorter array's m+1 partitions.
“O(log(n + 1) + 1) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: The n-based logarithm is a looser bound when m is much smaller; this fixed method searches the shorter array only.
“O(log(m + 1) + 1) time, O(log(m + 1) + 1) auxiliary space”: The partition search is iterative, so it does not retain one call frame per halving step.
